The event happened because of the way I acted
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 27-year-old Salvadoran-American animator who grew up in the Los Angeles area and built her career doing character work for a mid-sized animation studio in Burbank. She is presenting for her first course of psychological treatment following a period of sustained physical abuse by a former romantic partner that ended approximately fourteen months ago.

The relationship began when Valentina was twenty-four, and for its first several months it appeared unremarkable. The violence started gradually - a shove during an argument, an apology, a long quiet stretch - and then accelerated. By the relationship's second year, episodes of physical assault were occurring weekly, often triggered by disagreements that Valentina now replays obsessively in her mind. The incident she returns to most often took place in her own apartment on a Tuesday evening. She had pushed back during an argument about a work event she had attended without him. He struck her repeatedly, and she remembers most vividly that she did not leave the room. She stayed. She tried to calm him down. She said things she would not ordinarily say. She left the relationship only after a colleague noticed bruising on her forearm and sat with her until she agreed to call a family member.

In the months that followed, Valentina found herself preoccupied not primarily with fear of him, but with a quieter and more corrosive set of thoughts about herself. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt factual rather than interpretive, that something in her behaviour had invited what happened - that if she had spoken differently, acted less provocatively, been less stubborn, the violence would not have occurred. This conviction does not waver much in response to counter-evidence; when friends have gently challenged it, she has found their reassurances unconvincing. She is equally troubled by what she said and did during the worst episodes, moments when she believes she compromised values she had held since adolescence - around dignity, self-respect, and how a person ought to conduct themselves under pressure. She carries those moments as evidence of a self she no longer recognises and is not sure she can recover.

What frightens her most is the possibility that the person she was before - someone she describes as grounded, creative, and clear about who she was - is simply gone. She does not frame this as grief so much as diagnosis: she has permanently changed for the worse, and the change is structural, not circumstantial. This belief has quietly reorganised her daily life. At the studio, she works on character design, and the iterative, expressive nature of the work - which she once described as the part of her job she loved most - has become difficult to access. She has told her supervisor she is going through a rough patch, but the truth is that sitting with a character's emotional range, trying to render interiority on a face, now feels like an exercise she is no longer qualified to perform. She has missed two project deadlines in the past three months. A senior colleague she admires has been quietly reassigned to cover her work, and Valentina is aware of this and ashamed of it.

Socially, she has drawn back from the friends who knew her during the relationship, partly because their presence reminds her of a version of herself she finds difficult to look at directly. She has not started dating again and does not anticipate doing so. She describes her current life as functional but hollow - she goes to work, she meets her basic obligations, but she does not feel continuous with the person who chose this career and built this life.

What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her younger sister, who told her plainly that she seemed to have disappeared. Valentina sat with that for several weeks before making an appointment. She arrives at intake guarded but earnest, and what she says she most hopes for is not happiness exactly, but some evidence that she is not as permanently altered as she believes herself to be - that the animator who used to put something of herself into every character she drew might still, in some form, exist.
